name: Right Dislocation with a Pronoun

1.definition: Clarifies or reiterates a referent expressed by a pronoun in the preceding clause nucleus.
1.details: The following NP can disambiguate a pronoun or restate a referent that is already clear. CGEL contrasts a topic that is already evoked or accessible through the prior context with an attorney introduced for the first time, for which right dislocation is infelicitous. The observation concerns this pronoun-linked NP subtype.

examples.note: The final NP specifies the intended referent of him.
From a passage in which the book is already identified.

relatedConstructions.notes: The left pattern can introduce a new referent.
Extraposition has a different status for the pronoun and the final expression.

grounds.note: Gives a clause-first sequence with the co-referential final NP.

projection.target: Right dislocation favours an accessible referent. It can clarify a choice between already available referents, including when the pronoun is embedded.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts clarification, reiteration and discourse-new contexts. CASA notes the role of an active topic.

curious.title: Saying who you mean at the end
curious.summary: A speaker can use a pronoun and then add a noun phrase after the clause to say exactly who or what it was.
curious.body:
In I really like him, your dad, the word him already refers to someone. Then your dad is added at the end to make clear who. It can also simply restate a person or thing that's already clear, as in It's fascinating, this book.

The added phrase works best for something already in the conversation. A new person who hasn't been mentioned doesn't fit well in this slot: this dictionary notes that an attorney introduced for the first time is a poor fit here.
curious.try: Say something about a person or thing using only him, her or it, then add the name or noun at the end.

teacher.summary: Helps explain a tag-like noun phrase after a clause that repeats a pronoun's referent.
teacher.explain: In right dislocation, a clause with an overt personal pronoun is followed by an NP referring to the same thing: I really like him, your dad. The final NP can disambiguate the pronoun or restate a referent that is already clear. CGEL contrasts a topic that has been evoked or is accessible from the context with an attorney introduced for the first time, for which right dislocation is infelicitous. The observation concerns this pronoun-linked subtype. The pronoun can be embedded in the clause, and the pattern favours an accessible referent.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an antitopic or a tag NP. This dictionary also contrasts it with left dislocation, which can introduce a new referent.

contrasts.note: The pronoun alone; the listener must work out who him is.

contrasts.text: I really like him, your dad.
contrasts.note: The final NP specifies the intended referent.

watch_for: A learner might use the final NP to introduce someone new to the conversation, when the pattern fits an accessible referent.
A learner might drop the pronoun and keep only the final noun phrase.
teacher.activity: Give students two people in a picture. They say a sentence using him or her, and a partner adds a final noun phrase that says exactly who is meant.

child.hook: When you say "him", how does a friend know who you mean?
child.explain: You can say it first, then say the name at the end. I really like him, your dad. The end part tells who "him" is.
child.play: Say a sentence with him, her or it. Then add the person or thing at the end, after a little pause.
